## Applied Exercises

Work on these exercises in CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite, the working copy you made in Tutorial 9.1. Save the queries of each exercise in a script of their own, named after the exercise (such as `Ex 9.1.sql`), with a header comment like the one in Tutorial 9.3 and a comment above each query. The queries in this chapter only read data, so the exercises cannot change the database, but never type into the Browse Data tab while you work.

### Financial Accounting Exercises

**Exercise 9.1: Reviewing the Chart of Accounts**

**Table group:** Accounting Core

**Scenario.** Before the fiscal 2026 financial statements are finalized, the controller asks you to review the chart of accounts in the database. She wants to know how it is organized, which accounts carry a balance opposite to their type, and which accounts are no longer in use.

**Requirements.**

(1) List every account with its AccountID, AccountNumber, AccountName, AccountType, AccountSubType, ParentAccountID, NormalBalance, and IsActive, sorted by AccountNumber.

(2) Use DISTINCT to list the account types and, in a second query, the combinations of AccountType and AccountSubType. Describe how the subtypes divide each type.

(3) List the header accounts, whose AccountSubType is Header. Identify the ones that have no ParentAccountID and the ones that do, and explain what the difference means for the structure of the chart.

(4) List the accounts whose NormalBalance is Credit although their type is Asset or Expense, or Debit although their type is Liability, Equity, or Revenue. Use parentheses to group the conditions. Explain what kind of account each one is.

(5) List the inactive accounts (IsActive is 0). Two of them are named for manufacturing salaries and factory overhead. Use LIKE to find the active accounts whose names mention manufacturing, and suggest which of them records those costs instead.

(6) Write a short memo (one half page) to the controller summarizing the structure of the chart and anything that should be reviewed before year-end.

**Deliverable.** A script with the six queries and a half-page memo.

**Exercise 9.2: The Purchase Price Variance in the Ledger**

**Table group:** Accounting Core, Procure-to-Pay

**Scenario.** Cost of goods sold includes a second variance account, 5060 Purchase Price Variance. The controller asks for a first look at its postings in fiscal 2026, to learn what the account records and how it compares with the manufacturing variance.

**Requirements.**

(1) Find the AccountID of account 5060.

(2) List the distinct source document types of the account's postings in fiscal 2026, and identify the one that must be excluded from an analysis of the account. Explain why.

(3) Use DISTINCT to list the descriptions of the remaining postings. Explain the two kinds of cost the account records.

(4) List the postings of fiscal 2026 whose description records an unfavorable purchase variance, sorted by Debit from the largest down, and show the ten largest with their posting date and voucher number.

(5) Using the message pane, count the postings of each description. Explain what a credit to this account means.

(6) Write two or three sentences comparing how purchase price variance and manufacturing variance arise, based on the source documents that post to each account.

**Deliverable.** A script with the queries and a short comparison.

<!-- Instructor notes, Exercise 9.2: 5060 Purchase Price Variance is AccountID 55. Fiscal 2026 source types: PurchaseInvoice and
     JournalEntry; the JournalEntry row is closing entry JE-2026-000296, a credit of 176,011.36, which clears the account. PurchaseInvoice
     postings: 23,556 rows with three descriptions: "Record unfavorable purchase variance" 12,389 debits (167,063.83), "Record favorable
     purchase variance" 7,270 credits (57,497.25), and "Record nonrecoverable purchase tax" 3,897 debits (66,444.78); the net, 176,011.36,
     equals the close. The purchase variance is the invoice price against the purchase-order price at which the goods were received (the
     invoice clears goods received not invoiced, account 2020, at the receipt value); a credit means the supplier billed below the order
     price. The account also absorbs purchase tax that cannot be recovered. Largest unfavorable variance 796.29 (2026-01-31, voucher
     V0101-2026-020853); next 783.75 and 752.40. Purchase variance is recorded when a supplier invoice is posted; manufacturing variance
     when a work order closes, comparing actual with standard production cost. -->


### Managerial Accounting Exercises

**Exercise 9.3: Standard Cost Components of Manufactured Items**

**Table group:** Master Data, Manufacturing

**Scenario.** The manufacturing variance compares actual cost with standard cost, so the controller wants to understand how the standards are built before the variance is analyzed. She asks you for a review of the standard cost components of the items Charles River makes.

**Requirements.**

(1) List the items whose SupplyMode is Manufactured, with ItemCode, ItemName, ItemGroup, StandardCost, StandardLaborHoursPerUnit, StandardDirectLaborCost, StandardVariableOverheadCost, StandardFixedOverheadCost, and StandardConversionCost.

(2) Add a calculated column for the standard material cost, the part of StandardCost that is not conversion cost, and round it to two decimals.

(3) Write a query that returns any manufactured item whose direct labor, variable overhead, and fixed overhead do not add up to its standard conversion cost, after rounding to two decimals. Report the result.

(4) Add a calculated column for the standard labor rate per hour, StandardDirectLaborCost divided by StandardLaborHoursPerUnit, rounded to two decimals, and sort the items by it. Describe the range of rates.

(5) List the ten items with the highest standard conversion cost, and state which item groups they belong to.

**Deliverable.** A script with the queries and a short description of how the standards are built.

**Exercise 9.4: Open Work Orders at Year-End**

**Table group:** Manufacturing

**Scenario.** A work order's variance is recorded only when it closes, so the work orders still open at the end of fiscal 2026 hold variance that has not yet reached the ledger. The production manager and the controller want to know how many work orders are open, in what state, and how late they are.

**Requirements.**

(1) List the work orders with no ClosedDate, with their WorkOrderNumber, Status, ReleasedDate, DueDate, CompletedDate, and PlannedQuantity.

(2) Add two calculated columns: the year in each WorkOrderNumber, extracted with SUBSTR and converted with CAST, and the CompletedDate with the text not completed in place of a missing value, using COALESCE. Describe what the two columns show about the open work orders.

(3) Use DISTINCT to list the statuses of the open work orders. For each status, count the work orders with a separate query and the message pane.

(4) List the open work orders whose DueDate is on or before 2026-12-31, sorted by DueDate. Identify the oldest.

(5) Among them, list the work orders whose Status is Released, meaning that work has not started. Describe what you find.

(6) Write a short memo (one half page) to the production manager on the open work orders, and explain why their variance is not yet in the fiscal 2026 results.

**Deliverable.** A script with the queries and a half-page memo.

### Auditing Exercises

**Exercise 9.5: Shipments That Need Follow-Up**

**Table group:** Order-to-Cash

**Scenario.** In Tutorial 2.1 you found shipments with no tracking number and shipments still marked In Transit after their delivery date, working with filters in Excel. The audit senior asks you to repeat both tests with SQL, so that they can be saved and rerun at the next year-end.

**Requirements.**

(1) Use DISTINCT to list the values of Status and of ShippedBy in the Shipment table.

(2) List the shipments with no TrackingNumber, with their ShipmentNumber, ShipmentDate, ShippedBy, and Status, sorted by ShipmentDate. Report the number of rows and the range of dates.

(3) List the shipments whose Status is In Transit and whose DeliveryDate is before 2026-12-31, the last day of the data, sorted by DeliveryDate. Report the number of rows and the oldest DeliveryDate.

(4) Compare your results with your findings from Tutorial 2.1, and explain why the SQL version of the tests is easier to rerun.

(5) For each test, name the data quality dimension it addresses and suggest one question to ask the shipping team.

**Deliverable.** A script with the queries and a short comparison with Tutorial 2.1.

<!-- Instructor notes, Exercise 9.5: Status values Delivered (8,967) and In Transit (740); ShippedBy DHL Supply Chain, FedEx Freight,
     Private Fleet, UPS Freight. No TrackingNumber (NULL): 392 shipments, dated 2024-01-16 to 2026-12-31. In Transit with DeliveryDate
     before 2026-12-31: 739, the oldest delivered 2024-01-10 (one more In Transit shipment has a DeliveryDate on or after 2026-12-31). The
     SQL results equal the Excel filters of Tutorial 2.1. Dimensions: completeness (tracking number) and consistency or timeliness (status
     that contradicts the delivery date). The tests are saved as text and rerun with one click. -->


**Exercise 9.6: Missing Values in Time and Labor Records**

**Table group:** Manufacturing, Payroll and Time

**Scenario.** The manufacturing variance depends on the labor time recorded against work orders. Before the audit team relies on those records, the audit senior asks you to test them for missing values that could signal incomplete or unreliable time data.

**Requirements.**

(1) List the LaborTimeEntry rows whose LaborType is Direct Manufacturing and whose WorkOrderOperationID is missing. Show the employee, work order, work date, and hours.

(2) Use DISTINCT to list the values of ClockStatus in the TimeClockEntry table, and list the time clock entries with no ClockOutTime, showing `COALESCE(ClockOutTime, 'missing')` in place of the empty value.

(3) List the employees with a TerminationDate, with their EmploymentStatus and IsActive flag, and check whether the three columns agree.

(4) For each finding, explain why a missing value matters for the labor cost that reaches the manufacturing variance, and what you would ask the payroll or production team.

**Deliverable.** A script with the queries and a short list of findings with follow-up questions.
